questions.topic: Bank account dashboard and component composition
questions.question: What information should a customer account dashboard display, and how would you represent it using Angular components?

definition.text: Banking dashboards summarize authorized accounts, balances, and recent activity.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A banking user must understand available funds, account identity, recent activity and service status without opening several unrelated screens. A dashboard is a deliberate read-model and presentation boundary: it composes small independently testable components while the server remains authoritative about balances and ownership. Showing a current balance and an available balance explicitly avoids a dangerous implication that all booked funds are spendable.
motivation.historicalNote: Earlier account interfaces often presented a statement-like ledger first; digital banking dashboards foreground actionable balances, alerts and shortcuts while retaining transaction detail elsewhere. Exact terminology varies by bank, country and product.

problemSolved.before: One large component mixes account fetches, currency logic, masked identifiers, transaction rendering and transfer actions, making mistakes difficult to isolate.
problemSolved.after: Separate a dashboard shell from accessible AccountBalanceCard, RecentTransactions and AccountAlert components, using typed view models populated by authorized API endpoints.
benefits: Component responsibilities become easier to explain and test.
Loading, empty and error states can be explicit for each data area.
Sensitive identifiers can be consistently masked.
Available and posted amounts can be labeled accurately rather than conflated.

characteristics: Shows account nickname, masked identifier, currency and product type without exposing complete account numbers.
Distinguishes posted/current balance from available balance; pending holds and other restrictions may affect spendable funds.
Separately presents recent activity, pending items, service alerts and last-updated status.
Uses typed inputs and accessible currency/amount labeling in reusable components.
Treats API-provided monetary values as authoritative display data, not browser-computed banking balances.

simpleAnalogy.title: Car dashboard
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A car dashboard shows speed, fuel and warning lights in one place; it does not itself control the engine. Likewise an Angular account dashboard assembles views while backend systems enforce actual account rules.

industryExample.scenario: A fictional customer opens a current account with a posted balance of 12,000 INR and an available balance of 10,500 INR because 1,500 INR is held for a pending debit.
industryExample.implementation: An authenticated GET /api/accounts/summary returns server-authorized summaries in minor units; Angular maps each one into a balance card plus a recent-activity link. The UI displays the hold reason only if supplied safely by the API.
industryExample.businessImpact: Clear labels prevent customers from mistaking posted money for immediately spendable money; consistent errors reduce avoidable support calls.
constraints: The precise meaning of current, ledger, booked and available balances depends on product and bank policy.
No full PAN, account number or customer identity should be exposed in browser logs.
Dashboard display does not decide whether a transfer is allowed.

useCases: Show account overviews after secure login.
Display a read-only account snapshot in a customer portal.
Compose multiple account types without merging their currency values.
Present recent transactions and pending activity near their related balances.
Display actionable maintenance messages or service notices.

steps: Customer signs in using the identity system.
Angular dashboard requests GET /api/accounts/summary.
API authenticates and authorizes account ownership, then obtains a balance read model.
API returns posted/available values with currency, display alias and update timestamp.
Angular formats values, masks identifiers and renders card, alerts and recent-activity links.
When an error occurs, the dashboard shows a retry path without substituting stale values as current.

diagrams.title: Bank account dashboard and component composition: banking end-to-end workflow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Customer
  participant UI as Angular Dashboard
  participant API as Account API
  participant Auth as Authorization
  participant Ledger as Balance read model
  Customer->>UI: Open accounts page
  UI->>API: GET /api/accounts/summary
  API->>Auth: Verify session and account ownership
  Auth-->>API: Authorized account IDs
  API->>Ledger: Read posted and available balances
  Ledger-->>API: Balance snapshots
  API-->>UI: 200 account summaries
  UI-->>Customer: Labeled, masked account cards
diagrams.caption: Conceptual flow with fictional accounts; all authorization, monetary rules and persistence guarantees must be implemented and verified server-side.

codeExample.runtime: Angular standalone component. Pass only an authorized fictional AccountSummary from a parent; input values are demonstration read models, not financial posting logic.
codeExample.explanation: The child renders one immutable account summary supplied by its parent; the backend owns the balances and authorization. The divide-by-100 shortcut is appropriate only for this two-decimal INR demo, not every ISO currency. Do not derive spendable funds by subtracting arbitrary pending UI rows.

projectExperience.example: For the banking portfolio I would create account cards, a recent-activity widget and explicit available versus posted labels, using a mock API first and then an authorized NestJS endpoint.
evidenceToCollect: Screenshot of both balance labels with a pending hold fixture.
Component test verifying masked numbers and currency text.
API test proving a user cannot access another user’s account.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a portfolio proposal, not verified employment or completed-project experience. Replace with truthful implementation evidence after building and testing it.

pitfalls: Using a single ambiguous “Balance” label can cause wrong spending decisions.
Formatting minor units with a hardcoded /100 is wrong for currencies with 0 or 3 decimal places.
Showing complete account numbers or sensitive errors leaks data.
Assuming browser cards represent live ledger writes is incorrect.
Stale responses can be misread as fresh without update timestamps.
whenNotToUse: Do not calculate authoritative balance or transfer limits from displayed transaction rows.
Do not render unmasked account identifiers where product requirements prohibit it.
Do not aggregate unlike currencies into a total without an explicit FX model.

alternatives.name: Monolithic dashboard component
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to start but hard to isolate error states and tests.

alternatives.name: Server-composed dashboard endpoint
alternatives.bestFor: Several cards requiring synchronized read models
alternatives.tradeoff: Reduces browser fan-out but increases backend-for-frontend complexity.

alternatives.name: Independent card APIs
alternatives.tradeoff: More requests and mixed refresh times must be communicated.

testing.strategy: Use component fixture tests for labels and masking, contract tests for DTO shape, and backend authorization tests. Add accessibility assertions for headings and account context.

testCases.expected: Two separately labeled values render correctly for a pending-hold fixture.
Only the last permitted characters appear; full account ID is never displayed.
API returns only accounts owned by the authenticated principal.
The parent displays an explicit empty state, not fake zeros.

negativeCases: Simulate a malformed currency or missing timestamp and verify safe fallback behavior.
Simulate 403 and 500 without displaying protected information.
testing.verificationCommand: ng test && ng build; run API contract and authorization tests

intermediate: How would you prevent stale account snapshots during rapid navigation?
advanced: How would you profile dashboard API fan-out and choose a read model?
expert: How would you design multi-currency balance read models with auditability?

answer.finalTakeaway: A dashboard displays authorized account truth clearly; it never creates banking truth.

questions.topic: Typed transaction history and display conventions
questions.question: How would you display transaction history with amount, currency, date, type and status?

definition.text: Transaction history presents dated money movements with explicit statuses.

motivation.whyIntroduced: People need to reconcile what happened to their funds, separate pending activity from posted activity and find the relevant reference when speaking to support. A consistent transaction-row model prevents different screens from disagreeing about amounts, dates or statuses. Banking systems often distinguish authorization, posting, reversals and refunds; the UI must not flatten these into a misleading success label.
motivation.historicalNote: Electronic statements evolved from posted ledger entries toward mobile feeds that include pending items; a transaction feed may contain items not yet reflected in posted account balance.

problemSolved.before: UI screens concatenate ambiguous amount strings, infer pending status from dates, format currencies inconsistently and lose transaction references.
problemSolved.after: A typed API contract supplies id, occurredAt, amountMinor, currency, direction, status and description, while Angular formats and displays the fields accessibly.
benefits: Shows positive and negative cash flow with consistent conventions.
Makes pending versus posted status understandable.
Supports accessible, sortable transaction rows.
Preserves backend-issued references for support and reconciliation.

characteristics: Stable transaction id is used as a tracking key, never array index.
Amount is modeled in minor units plus ISO currency; signed versus direction conventions must be clearly defined.
Timestamp is formatted using an explicit user or product timezone; posting date may differ from transaction date.
Status is a documented domain enum, not inferred from HTTP success.
Descriptions are rendered as text; sensitive merchant and payer details are minimized.

simpleAnalogy.title: Parcel tracking
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A parcel shows when it was accepted, dispatched and delivered. A money movement similarly has a timeline and a status, but processing success does not always mean final posting.

industryExample.scenario: A debit-card purchase for INR 849.00 appears as pending after authorization and later as posted. A reversal can be a distinct record, depending on the bank contract.
industryExample.implementation: An authorized GET /api/accounts/{id}/transactions returns paginated records with a backend-defined status enum. Angular renders a responsive list with a status label and a localized date, and uses a stable id for track.
industryExample.businessImpact: Customers can differentiate an unsettled hold from a completed debit and locate a transaction without contacting support.
constraints: The backend must scope the requested account to the authenticated user.
A pending authorization may expire or change amount before posting.
Timezone and date conventions must be specified in the API contract.

useCases: Customer transaction feeds.
Account statements and export previews.
Support-agent transaction investigations with proper access controls.
Reconciliation read-only consoles.
Refund and reversal activity lists.

steps: Customer selects an account.
Angular requests a paginated transaction page.
Backend checks account ownership and filters records by authorized account.
Backend returns status, timestamps, amountMinor, currency, id and safe description.
Angular maps the domain DTO to accessible rows; stable track keys preserve row identity.
Customer expands a row to see reference and permitted detail, not hidden personal data.

diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Customer
  participant List as Angular Transaction List
  participant API as Transactions API
  participant Store as Transaction read store
  Customer->>List: Open activity
  List->>API: GET /accounts/{id}/transactions?page=1
  API->>API: Authenticate and check account access
  API->>Store: Read authorized transaction page
  Store-->>API: Items and pagination metadata
  API-->>List: Transaction DTO page
  List-->>Customer: Amount, date, direction and status
diagrams.caption: Conceptual flow with fictional accounts; all authorization, monetary rules and persistence guarantees must be implemented and verified server-side.

codeExample.runtime: Angular standalone component with a typed authorized INR list passed from its parent; real systems also need pagination and a defined timezone.
codeExample.explanation: The reusable list concerns presentation; API pagination and account ownership checks remain server-side. `@for` tracks each transaction by stable id. If the product supports multiple currencies, use a currency-aware formatter instead of assuming two decimal places.

projectExperience.example: In a simulated banking project I would implement a typed transaction list, load a small read-only page from NestJS and attach a detail view for references and status explanation.
evidenceToCollect: Fixture proving pending and posted are displayed differently.
Snapshot or component test proving negative debit values keep their sign.
Authorization test denying cross-account transaction browsing.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a portfolio proposal, not verified employment or completed-project experience. Replace with truthful implementation evidence after building and testing it.

pitfalls: Changing the displayed status to posted before actual settlement is misleading.
Parsing timestamps without timezone assumptions can shift dates.
Index-based tracking can reuse wrong row UI on sort or updates.
A transaction total is not necessarily the ledger balance.
Displaying raw merchant payload as HTML risks injection.
whenNotToUse: Do not decide whether a transaction is posted based on the HTTP request outcome.
Do not assume every transaction is a debit or that all currencies have two decimals.
Do not request arbitrary accounts without enforcing backend ownership.

alternatives.name: Card-based history
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple scanning but less suitable for dense reconciliation data.

alternatives.name: Data table
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires careful mobile and keyboard support.

alternatives.name: Server-rendered statement
alternatives.tradeoff: Not as interactive as a live transaction feed.

testing.strategy: Test status rendering, signed amount conventions, stable row identity, date formatting and page boundaries; use integration tests for authorized account scoping.

testCases.expected: Label pending without claiming settled or posted.
Signed amount and currency are represented consistently.
Shows an explicit empty state.
Reordering records preserves id-to-row association.

negativeCases: A missing or unknown status must not silently render as posted.
Malformed time values should not produce a misleading date; validate DTOs at boundaries.
testing.verificationCommand: ng test && ng build; run transaction API contract tests

questions.question: How would you build a bank transaction search with account filters and date-range selection?

definition.text: Banking search combines authorized account selection with bounded dates.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Once a customer has months of activity, scrolling a single unfiltered list is too slow and confusing. A search form narrows results by account and date and gives meaningful feedback about invalid ranges. The important boundary is that client filters improve usability but cannot constrain security: the API still checks access to the selected account and validates date parameters.
motivation.historicalNote: Statement pages originally relied on monthly paging; interactive web search adds account selection, date ranges and server-side pagination. For larger data volumes, server filtering is preferable to downloading all transactions.

problemSolved.before: The browser downloads every transaction, filters by string dates and account IDs locally, and accidentally shows data the user is not authorized to access.
problemSolved.after: Angular validates selected accounts and ISO date strings, submits sanitized query parameters and displays the page returned by a server that performs authorization, date validation and pagination.
benefits: Account selection is derived from authorized account choices.
Start and end dates have a documented inclusive calendar-date contract.
The client rejects start date after end date before submission.
The backend revalidates parameters and applies access-control filtering.
Requests use typed DTOs and explicit loading and error states.

characteristics: Uses typed Reactive Forms controls with required-field validation.
Uses zero-padded YYYY-MM-DD date values with an explicitly defined range contract.
Sends account/date filters via HttpParams instead of downloading an entire history.
Leaves authorization and query validation to the backend.
Separately renders loading, results, empty and error states.

simpleAnalogy.title: Library search desk
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Instead of reading every book, a person asks for books from one section during a certain publication period. The library still decides which records they are permitted to request.

industryExample.scenario: A customer selects their salary account and searches debits from 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-31 to review spending before budgeting.
industryExample.implementation: Angular displays a select built from authorized accounts and date inputs, checks YYYY-MM-DD ordering, and calls GET /api/transactions with accountId, from, to, and page. The backend validates access and UTC/calendar boundaries and returns only permitted records.
industryExample.businessImpact: The customer sees a smaller auditable set of transactions and understands why a result is empty versus unavailable.
constraints: Demo assumes ISO date inputs and a fixed application date-range convention; production contracts must define timezone inclusivity.
Never accept arbitrary account IDs as proof of permission.
Never expose all customer transaction history to support browser filtering.

useCases: Search transaction history by month or billing period.
Filter across different customer-owned accounts.
Support spending review and downloadable statement requests.
Investigate a known transaction around a merchant date.
Page through large histories efficiently.

steps: Customer selects an account and start/end dates.
Angular verifies account selection and date ordering.
Client constructs encoded query parameters and issues GET /api/transactions.
Server authenticates and checks ownership of accountId.
Server validates date boundaries and runs a filtered paginated query.
Response returns typed transactions; UI renders success/empty/error states without fabricating data.

diagrams.title: Transaction filtering and date-range search: banking end-to-end workflow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Customer
  participant Form as Angular search form
  participant API as Transaction API
  participant Auth as Account authorization
  participant DB as Transaction store
  Customer->>Form: Select account and date range
  Form->>Form: Validate ordering and format
  Form->>API: GET /transactions?accountId=...&from=...&to=...
  API->>Auth: Verify account ownership
  Auth-->>API: Allowed or denied
  API->>DB: Filter authorized records and paginate
  DB-->>API: Transaction page
  API-->>Form: Results or HTTP error
  Form-->>Customer: Render list, empty state or error
diagrams.caption: Conceptual flow with fictional accounts; all authorization, monetary rules and persistence guarantees must be implemented and verified server-side.

codeExample.runtime: Angular standalone component; requires HttpClient configuration and /api/transactions backend. For learning only: hardcoded authorized account option, no pagination, and previous overlapping requests could still complete out of order.
codeExample.explanation: The FormGroup enforces required controls, then date ordering is checked explicitly before creating HttpParams. The server must validate the same boundaries and account ownership. A later Intermediate exercise should use switchMap or request-id guards so older searches cannot overwrite newer results.

projectExperience.example: For the banking portfolio, I would build the search UI on top of a mock endpoint, add authorization-aware account choices and document the server-side filter contract before connecting a database.
evidenceToCollect: UI test capturing a valid account and from/to query.
Backend test denying an account not owned by the user.
Screen recording of invalid date-range feedback and no-results state.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a portfolio proposal, not verified employment or completed-project experience. Replace with truthful implementation evidence after building and testing it.

pitfalls: Lexicographic comparison works only for valid, zero-padded ISO YYYY-MM-DD strings.
A client date-range validator does not provide backend security or input validation.
Repeated submissions can allow old results to overwrite fresh ones in this beginner implementation.
Unlimited result sets can slow the browser and expose excessive data.
A date without a defined timezone cannot reliably represent all posting intervals.
whenNotToUse: Do not download complete account histories for browser-side searching.
Do not trust the accountId query parameter for authorization.
Do not silently change the user’s timezone or inclusive date semantics.

alternatives.name: Server-side paged filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs a stable query contract and backend indexes.

alternatives.name: Client-side filtering
alternatives.tradeoff: Cannot scale or provide server authorization; inappropriate for full banking history.

alternatives.name: RxJS switchMap search
alternatives.bestFor: Rapidly changing filters and live search
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires deliberate stream design and API cancellation semantics.

testing.strategy: Use form tests for required fields and ordering; mock HTTP requests for params and error handling; perform API authorization and range-contract tests separately.

testCases.expected: Exactly one GET contains accountId, from and to.
UI displays validation message and sends no HTTP request.
A successful [] response shows no-results state.
A non-sensitive error appears and loading clears.

negativeCases: Craft a request with an accountId owned by another customer; backend must deny access.
Submit overlapping searches to document the stale-response weakness before the Intermediate improvement.

questions.topic: Shared balance data and duplicate network requests
questions.question: What problems arise when two components independently fetch and display the same account balance?

definition.text: Independent balance requests can create duplicate work and inconsistency.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A banking overview and header might each call the same account endpoint. Even if both are permitted, separate network requests can return at different times, render different snapshots, waste bandwidth and complicate loading and failure behavior. Shared read-only state should have clear ownership and invalidation, while the backend remains responsible for ledger correctness.
motivation.historicalNote: As single-page applications gained multiple widgets, independently fetching the same resource became a common source of duplicate calls and stale displays; service-level caching or server-composed read models can coordinate those reads.

problemSolved.before: AccountBalanceCard and HeaderBadge each subscribe independently to HttpClient.get, so two requests may return different versions and show conflicting totals.
problemSolved.after: An injectable account-summary query service deduplicates callers using a shared Observable; a single refresh invalidates the snapshot for the next read.
benefits: Less unnecessary network traffic for the same snapshot.
Components can subscribe to the same loaded response.
One location for error handling and refresh policy.
Easier investigation of conflicting balance displays.

characteristics: Angular HttpClient Observables are cold: independent subscriptions commonly issue independent requests.
shareReplay can multicast a response; the refresh and error-cache strategy must be explicit.
A shared cached snapshot has a freshness contract, not permanent financial truth.
The injection scope determines whether callers really share the same cache instance.
Server-side account authorization and balance calculation are unchanged.

simpleAnalogy.title: Two weather apps
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Two screens taking weather readings at different moments may show slightly different values. Sharing one dated report makes them consistent, but you still need to refresh it when conditions change.

industryExample.scenario: A banking portal header and account home both display available INR 10,500; a temporary authorization hold occurs between two separate requests, making one show INR 10,500 and the other INR 9,000.
industryExample.implementation: Both widgets inject one root-provided AccountSummaryQuery and subscribe to the same in-flight result. On explicit refresh the service invalidates the snapshot, causing a new authorized API read.
industryExample.businessImpact: Fewer duplicate requests and clearer freshness labeling reduce contradictory customer-facing balance displays.
constraints: Read model may become outdated due to external card and transfer events.
Do not claim this cache provides transaction consistency.
Access to bank account data must be checked on every backend request.

useCases: Share account summaries between header and dashboard.
Deduplicate account detail requests among multiple widgets.
Coordinate manual refresh after a simulated transfer.
Reduce repeated requests caused by multiple AsyncPipe subscriptions.
Centralize read-model error mapping.

steps: Header and dashboard independently request account summary.
Angular DI supplies the same root-scoped AccountSummaryQuery.
First caller starts an HttpClient GET; shareReplay multicasts the result.
Second subscriber receives the same in-flight or cached snapshot.
A transfer completion or refresh action invalidates the local cache.
Next subscriber triggers a fresh authorized read; the backend remains authoritative.

diagrams.title: Shared balance data and duplicate network requests: banking end-to-end workflow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Customer
  participant Header as Header widget
  participant Dashboard as Dashboard widget
  participant Query as Shared AccountSummaryQuery
  participant API as Account API
  Customer->>Header: Open portal
  Header->>Query: get()
  Query->>API: GET /api/accounts/summary
  Dashboard->>Query: get()
  Note over Query,API: One in-flight request is shared
  API-->>Query: Authorized account summary
  Query-->>Header: Same snapshot
  Query-->>Dashboard: Same snapshot
  Customer->>Dashboard: Refresh
  Dashboard->>Query: invalidate()
  Note over Query: Next get() fetches again
diagrams.caption: Conceptual flow with fictional accounts; all authorization, monetary rules and persistence guarantees must be implemented and verified server-side.

codeExample.runtime: Angular injectable service; requires HttpClient and an authenticated banking read API. Current demo assumes one authorized identity and explicit refresh; production code must handle sign-out and account/tenant switching.
codeExample.explanation: HttpClient gets are cold. Placing shareReplay around a lazily initialized request lets header and dashboard reuse the same result. Clearing `cached$` before a new request triggers a new GET; this simple cache does not guarantee monotonic snapshots or protect against in-flight old results after identity changes.

projectExperience.example: In the simulated banking project I would make both the navigation badge and dashboard consume a single AccountSummaryQuery, then add refresh after a transfer or account change and test request counts.
evidenceToCollect: HTTP mock verifying two subscribers cause one GET.
UI screenshot where header and dashboard have the same response timestamp.
Logout or account-switch test verifying identity-specific cache is cleared.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a portfolio proposal, not verified employment or completed-project experience. Replace with truthful implementation evidence after building and testing it.

pitfalls: Unbounded cache lifetime leaves financial data stale indefinitely.
Providing the service separately in each component defeats shared in-memory caching.
shareReplay with refCount false may keep a slow request running after consumers unsubscribe.
In-flight stale responses after user/account switching need generation or identity checks.
A cached value is not proof that the customer can initiate a transfer.
whenNotToUse: Do not use browser-cached balances to authorize transfers or overdrafts.
Do not share an account cache across authenticated identities or tenants.
Do not assume shareReplay makes POST transfers idempotent.

alternatives.bestFor: Shared current display state with explicit refresh
alternatives.tradeoff: Must coordinate async request lifecycle and stale responses.

alternatives.name: One server-composed summary endpoint
alternatives.bestFor: Multiple dashboard cards with related freshness
alternatives.tradeoff: Aggregates backend responsibilities and can increase coupling.

alternatives.name: Per-component requests
alternatives.bestFor: Independent resources or genuinely different freshness needs
alternatives.tradeoff: Can duplicate calls and show different read timestamps.

testing.strategy: Use HttpTestingController to prove multicasting and invalidation, a fake response to check visible timestamp consistency, and identity-switch tests against cache leakage.

testCases.expected: Exactly one GET is issued for both subscribers before refresh.
After invalidate(), a new get() issues a new GET.
The error reaches subscribers and the next get() can retry.
Header and dashboard receive a shared service instance.

negativeCases: Simulate sign-out and login as another user; production design must not reuse the old account cache.

questions.topic: Banking API failure and user-friendly error recovery
questions.question: How should an Angular application handle a failed account-summary API request?

definition.text: Account API failures require clear states and safe recovery.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Account summaries are sensitive, high-trust information. A missing response cannot be quietly replaced with zero or treated as a successful account state. The user needs a clear explanation that the current balance is unavailable, safe retry where appropriate, and no leakage of authentication details or server exceptions. HTTP status and network errors provide diagnostic signals but the UI must communicate them safely.
motivation.historicalNote: As enterprise apps moved from full-page server navigation to independent API widgets, explicitly modeling loading, success, empty and error became necessary to avoid ambiguous blank panels.

problemSolved.before: A failed GET leaves the spinner running, shows a fabricated zero balance, logs sensitive errors, or blindly retries unauthorized requests forever.
problemSolved.after: The component owns a small state machine: loading, success, empty/unavailable and error. It distinguishes unauthorized (401), forbidden (403), unexpected server failures (5xx) and network errors (status 0), then offers safe actions.
benefits: A loading state is explicit and always exits on completion or error.
401 means authentication context is missing/invalid; redirect policy belongs to central identity handling.
403 means the authenticated identity lacks required permission; retrying the same request does not fix it.
5xx and network failures produce a safe message and optional deliberate retry.
No failed response is shown as a confirmed monetary amount.

characteristics: Models idle, loading, ready and error as distinct states.
Maps 401, 403, transport failures and server failures to safe messages.
Never substitutes an error result with a fabricated money amount.
Offers controlled retry for transient read errors rather than indefinite loops.
Uses observable teardown to avoid post-destruction component updates.

simpleAnalogy.title: ATM temporarily offline
simpleAnalogy.explanation: If an ATM cannot connect to the bank, it should not pretend your balance is zero. It says the information is temporarily unavailable and offers a sensible next step.

industryExample.scenario: A customer opens their balance widget while the account service returns HTTP 503 during maintenance, then recovers on a later attempt.
industryExample.implementation: Angular calls GET /api/accounts/summary and renders a loading state. On 503 or network interruption, it displays “Balance temporarily unavailable” and a Retry button. On 401, it asks the user to reauthenticate through an appropriate auth flow; on 403 it shows access denied.
industryExample.businessImpact: Customers are less likely to act on wrong amounts and support teams can correlate incidents through sanitized request identifiers.
constraints: The backend enforces account authorization and returns safe error codes.
Do not expose tokens, raw exception traces or internal account identifiers.
Retry is not suitable for all errors or all operation types; this case is a read-only GET.

useCases: Unavailable bank balance cards.
Transaction list request failures.
Temporary maintenance pages in authenticated portals.
Recoverable connectivity errors on mobile networks.
Clear 401 versus 403 error treatment.

steps: Customer opens account dashboard.
Component enters loading state and requests account summary.
Backend may return 200, 401, 403, 503 or the transport may fail.
Component maps the outcome to explicit state without inventing values.
For recoverable read failures, customer can retry after service recovery.
Tests simulate each failure and assert no stale/sensitive data is shown as a fresh balance.

diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Customer
  participant UI as Account Summary UI
  participant API as Account API
  Customer->>UI: Open dashboard
  UI->>API: GET /api/accounts/summary
  alt Success
    API-->>UI: 200 authorized summary
    UI-->>Customer: Show updated balances
  else Unauthenticated
    API-->>UI: 401
    UI-->>Customer: Sign in again
  else Forbidden
    API-->>UI: 403
    UI-->>Customer: Access unavailable
  else Server or network error
    API-->>UI: 503 or network failure
    UI-->>Customer: Temporary error and Retry
    Customer->>UI: Retry
    UI->>API: GET /api/accounts/summary
  end
diagrams.caption: Conceptual flow with fictional accounts; all authorization, monetary rules and persistence guarantees must be implemented and verified server-side.

codeExample.runtime: Angular standalone component with a sample /api/accounts/summary endpoint and explicit discriminated-union state; account money is displayed as minor units for clarity.
codeExample.explanation: The discriminated union ensures a failed response cannot masquerade as a valid Summary. The view can separately distinguish login-required, forbidden and retryable conditions. For complete production UX, wire retryable to the Retry control and add centralized authentication handling and consistent request tracing.

projectExperience.example: In the banking portfolio I would simulate HTTP 401, 403, 503 and network errors, verify that amounts are hidden when unavailable and demonstrate a retry after 503 recovery.
evidenceToCollect: Screenshot of safe error messages without raw backend data.
Backend log correlation using a non-sensitive trace ID.
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a portfolio proposal, not verified employment or completed-project experience. Replace with truthful implementation evidence after building and testing it.

pitfalls: Rendering zero on API failure confuses unavailable data with genuine zero balance.
Blind retries on 401/403 can create request loops or mask access problems.
Persisting old balances without freshness labeling is misleading.
Console logging raw errors may leak user or account details.
Retrying a financial POST is not equivalent to retrying a GET summary.
whenNotToUse: Do not silently assume a failed account read means an empty account.
Do not automatically retry transfer-creation requests without verified idempotency guarantees.
Do not put raw backend exception messages or access tokens into customer-facing UI.

alternatives.name: Central global error boundary
alternatives.tradeoff: Cannot replace context-specific bank account error states.

testing.strategy: Use an HTTP test controller or service stub to assert loading, success and failure transitions. Verify no sensitive balance appears after a failed refresh; add e2e network interruption cases and backend access tests.

testCases.expected: Visible state contains returned authenticated summary.
Displays sign-in guidance, not a generic retry loop.
Displays access unavailable; does not reveal other accounts.
Displays a safe temporary failure message and retryable state.
Displays temporary network failure rather than zero balance.

negativeCases: Return a malformed DTO and verify runtime validation or a safe fallback is planned.
Simulate an error arriving after sign-out and ensure no account data is restored to a different user session.
